name: Markley Group

profile.address: 2, Prince Avenue, Bleachery, Lowell, Middlesex County, Massachusetts, 01825
profile.reading:
This 352,000-square-foot mission-critical data center at 2 Prince Avenue in the Bleachery section of Lowell, Massachusetts, is operated by Markley Group, a Boston-based colocation and connectivity company founded in 1991 by Jeff Markley, who is widely credited with helping originate the modern "carrier hotel" concept -- a facility where multiple network carriers interconnect alongside colocated customer equipment. Markley's flagship building, One Summer Street in Boston (920,000 square feet, opened 1998), is the company's best-known site, but the Lowell facility is its second Massachusetts data center and, per Markley's own materials, a comparably serious mission-critical building rather than a satellite location: it was built in 2015 on the former site of the Prince Macaroni/Prince Spaghetti factory, after Markley completed environmental remediation of the industrial site. The company states the Lowell building offers highly secured white space with 2N redundant UPS and generator backup, three physically diverse dark-fiber routes into Boston, and connections to two separate electric utility substations for power resiliency. Markley does not publish an exact power-capacity figure for Lowell specifically, though its comparable Boston facility is reported to run up to 30 megawatts. Local reporting -- including a CBS Boston investigation that gained rare interior access -- describes a facility serving more than 100 customers spanning hospitals, universities, police departments, financial firms, and life-sciences companies, running thousands of servers and storing many petabytes of data, staffed by roughly a dozen union electricians and a dozen pipefitters day to day, with crews expanding to 80-100 workers during major infrastructure projects. Neighboring residents have nicknamed the black-clad building "the dungeon," and have raised recurring complaints about the constant hum of its industrial air-conditioning units and about emergency-generator exhaust venting toward nearby homes; the same reporting found the facility's water use, drawn from utility billing records, running between roughly 60,000 and 120,000 gallons per day for cooling. Markley states it has never experienced a primary power outage across more than fifteen years of operating its Massachusetts data centers.

Markley's two Massachusetts buildings illustrate a common pattern in the colocation industry: rather than building many small facilities, an established operator concentrates investment in a small number of very large, deeply redundant campuses and grows by expanding capacity within them over time. The Lowell site's siting on a remediated former food-manufacturing property is also typical of the sector, since large industrial parcels with existing heavy electrical service and highway or rail access are attractive to data-center developers precisely because they avoid the cost of building that infrastructure from scratch.

reading:
Markley Group is a privately held colocation operator founded in 1991 by Jeff Markley, best known for its Boston carrier hotel at One Summer Street, which the company describes as 920,000 square feet of secured white and mechanical space in service since 1998. The single facility this registry holds for Markley is not that building. It is the company's Lowell site at 2 Prince Avenue in Middlesex County, a 352,000 square foot conversion of the former Prince pasta mill that has operated as a data centre since 2015, and it has become the most closely documented data centre in Massachusetts because its neighbours took it to court.

The local and regulatory record is unusually full. On the utility side, Massachusetts Electric Company doing business as National Grid filed a Notice of Project Change under the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act, EEA file number 15988, noticed on 22 October 2020 with a certificate issued on 23 November 2020, covering reconductoring of the 2385 distribution line at 23 kilovolts across Lowell, Billerica and Tewksbury between the Wigginville and Quebec Street substations, extended by ten additional poles and roughly 1,175 feet along an MBTA railroad right of way, to serve the Prince Avenue building. That is utility supply work and says nothing about the building's IT load.

On the standby side the numbers are separate again. The city approved 31 generators about a decade ago, 23 were operating as of 2026 reporting, and on 3 July 2025 the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection approved a non major comprehensive plan covering diesel backup generators and cooling towers that would bring the site to 27 operating generators and 16 cooling towers, with on site storage of about 250,000 gallons of diesel. These are standby diesel and heat rejection counts, not capacity, and no critical IT megawatt figure has ever been published for either the Lowell or the Boston building.

The building sits in Lowell's Sacred Heart and Back Central neighbourhoods, abutted by homes, a park and a baseball field, within a state designated environmental justice area. Eight residents were granted standing in the air permit appeal on 27 August 2025. A hearing officer recommended approval that December and the commissioner upheld the permit in early 2026. In late April 2026 residents represented by the Conservation Law Foundation, the Yale Environmental Justice Law and Advocacy Clinic and Fitch Law Partners filed suit in Massachusetts Superior Court, the first case of its kind in the state, and on 10 August 2026 a judge paused the four generators not yet installed. Markley says it completed every analysis the department required and expects the permit to stand. Lowell has separately adopted a one year moratorium on new data centres, which does not reach this building.
